titre: The VCR Hollywood Tried to Ban
accroche: In 1984, the U.S. Supreme Court refuses to hold Sony liable for pirate copies made with the Betamax, sold as capable of honest uses.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 10, 1975, Sony launches the first consumer videocassette recorder, the Betamax, in Japan, before releasing it in the United States later that year, in November. The device lets anyone with a television set record a live broadcast to watch later, what the Supreme Court's opinion will call “time-shifting.” In 1976, Universal City Studios and Walt Disney Productions sue Sony in a federal court in California. They go after no particular viewer: they target the manufacturer itself, on the grounds that selling a device that makes copying possible amounts to organizing the infringement of millions of protected works.

The district court sides with Sony in 1979. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses that judgment in 1981 and holds Sony liable. The case goes up to the Supreme Court, which rules on January 17, 1984, by five votes to four, in Sony's favor.

## A principle borrowed from patent law

American copyright law of the time says nothing about a manufacturer who has copied nothing itself. The Court looks elsewhere for its rule, in a patent-law doctrine called the staple article of commerce rule: selling a product that can be used in a way that infringes a patent does not make the seller guilty of contributory infringement, as long as the product is also substantially suited to uses that infringe nothing. The opinion, written by Justice John Paul Stevens, carries this reasoning over into copyright law: it is enough that the device be capable of substantial noninfringing uses to rule out liability for the one who sells it.

The remaining question was whether the Betamax had any. The Court holds that it did, starting with time-shifting itself: recording a program to watch it once, later, at home, is in its view a fair use, notably because some rights holders expressly consent to having their programs recorded, and because nothing proves measurable economic harm to the studios.

## The same argument, a different tool

The vote is a close one: four justices would have held Sony liable. The fate of the VCR, and with it an entire emerging consumer electronics industry, came down to a single vote.

Forty years later, the same argument is back in court over tools no one imagined in 1984: text and image generators built on artificial intelligence. Publishing houses and news agencies are suing their makers, arguing that the tools allow protected works to be reproduced; the companies targeted answer, like Sony before them, that their tools are also suited to uses that infringe nothing. The test of substantial noninfringing uses has not changed its name since 1984. What remains open is what exactly counts as substantial when the tool in question can produce a number of works that no VCR could have recorded in a lifetime.

citation.texte: the sale of copying equipment, like the sale of other articles of commerce, does not constitute contributory infringement if the product is widely used for legitimate, unobjectionable purposes. Indeed, it need merely be capable of substantial noninfringing uses.
citation.source: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc., 464 U.S. 417, opinion of the Court, January 17, 1984

carte.punch: A tool capable of honest use doesn't make its maker liable, even when others misuse it.
carte.idee: In 1984, the U.S. Supreme Court refuses to hold Sony liable for pirate copies made with the Betamax. It rules that a VCR capable of legitimate recordings is enough to protect its manufacturer, even if some users employ it to infringe.
carte.source_courte: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios, 1984

quiz.question: Why does the U.S. Supreme Court refuse to hold Sony liable for copies made with the Betamax?
choix: Universal and Disney had not registered their works before they aired, which deprived them of any right to sue
The VCR is capable of substantial noninfringing uses, which is enough to rule out its manufacturer's liability
Sony had obtained a blanket license from the television networks before marketing the device
Congress had just passed a law explicitly exempting home recording from any lawsuit
quiz.explication: The Court borrows from patent law the staple article of commerce rule: a product capable of substantial noninfringing uses does not make its manufacturer liable, even if some users employ it to copy illegally. No statute exempted home recording, and nothing in the case rests on a license or a failure to register the works.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the result of the Supreme Court's vote on January 17, 1984?
choix: Five votes to four, in favor of Sony
Nine votes to zero, unanimously in favor of Sony
Six votes to three, in favor of Universal and Disney
Five votes to four, in favor of Universal and Disney
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The vote is a close one: four justices would have held Sony liable, but the five-vote majority sides with it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the Supreme Court borrow the principle of substantial noninfringing uses from?
choix: From trademark law, applied by analogy to copyright
From an international treaty on intellectual property
From a patent-law doctrine on staple articles of commerce
From a 1976 federal statute on home recording
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Copyright law said nothing about a manufacturer who had copied nothing itself; the Court looks for its rule in a patent-law doctrine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which court first rules in favor of the studios, before the Supreme Court decides otherwise?
choix: The district court in California, in 1979
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, in 1981
The California State Supreme Court
The U.S. Congress, by a 1980 resolution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The district court had sided with Sony as early as 1979; it is the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals that reverses it in 1981.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Court hold that time-shifting is a fair use?
choix: Because a 1976 federal statute explicitly authorized home recording
Because Sony paid the studios a royalty for each device sold
Because time-shifting concerned only works in the public domain
Because some rights holders consented to it and no economic harm was proven
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court finds that some rights holders expressly consented to recording, and that nothing proved measurable economic harm.
